The Story of Sagardatt the Monk

I bow to Lord Jinendra, who sees and knows the three worlds through the bright eyes of omniscience, and I write the story of Sagardatt, who became a monk out of fear of the greed for wealth.

Once upon a time, many merchants' sons — Dhanmitra, Dhandatt, and others — set out from Kaushambi for Rajgriha on a trading journey. In a dense forest along the way, thieves robbed them of all their goods and possessions. Truly, those who have no merit in their store suffer loss in whatever they undertake.

Having seized the merchants' wealth, the thieves' minds turned corrupt. Each one wanted the entire hoard for himself and none wanted to share with the others. In this greed they began plotting against one another's lives. That night, when they sat down to eat, someone had mixed poison in the food. They all ate it and perished on the spot — even the one who had added the poison died, having eaten it himself by mistake.

Among the merchants, only one survived — a young man named Sagardatt. He was spared because he had taken a vow never to eat or drink after nightfall. Seeing all the thieves lying dead, killed by their own greed for the very wealth they had stolen, Sagardatt was struck with profound renunciation. He understood that the lust for wealth is a poison more deadly than any substance — it had destroyed all these men in a single night, and had he been attached to his goods, he too would have perished alongside them.

Sagardatt left all the wealth lying there in the forest without a backward glance. He sought out a monk and took initiation as a mendicant. He reflected that all the plays of the world are causes of suffering, and that life is as fleeting as a flash of lightning, destroyed in an instant. He became a monk of the highest conduct, practising austerities and meditation with unwavering dedication.

Through his spiritual practice, Sagardatt destroyed his karmas and attained liberation. The vow of not eating at night — a simple practice — saved his life, and the sight of the dead thieves taught him the supreme lesson that wealth is the root of violence and that true peace lies only in renunciation.

This story teaches that greed is the greatest poison. The thieves killed each other over stolen wealth that none of them could enjoy. Sagardatt, through a simple vow and a moment of clear seeing, turned away from the very wealth that had destroyed his companions and found the path to eternal peace. May the monk Sagardatt bless all noble souls.
